meta.title: A cognitive profile of multi-sensory imagery, memory and dreaming in aphantasia
meta.domain: Cognitive neuroscience — mental imagery, individual differences, aphantasia
meta.overview: Large-sample (N=667) questionnaire study profiling self-identified aphantasics against two control cohorts across visual and non-visual imagery, autobiographical memory, dreaming, and spatial ability. Aphantasia is shown to be frequently multi-sensory (not purely visual), associated with weaker episodic memory and reduced/less vivid dreaming, while spatial imagery and navigation are preserved.
meta.abstract: Aphantasia is the inability to voluntarily generate visual mental imagery. In the largest cognitive profiling to date (N=667), self-reported aphantasics showed markedly reduced visual imagery vividness (VVIQ), reduced imagery across non-visual sensory modalities, lower vividness of episodic autobiographical memory, and fewer/less vivid dreams, while spatial imagery and navigation were preserved. Most report a lifelong (congenital) rather than acquired condition.

claims.statement: Aphantasic individuals report far lower visual imagery vividness than controls (VVIQ 17.94 vs 58.12; r=0.87).
Aphantasia is associated with reduced imagery across non-visual sensory modalities (auditory, tactile, etc.).
Aphantasics report lower ability to vividly remember specific life events (episodic autobiographical memory).
Aphantasic individuals experience fewer and less sensorily vivid dreams than controls.
Spatial imagery and spatial navigation ability are preserved in aphantasia.
Aphantasia in this sample is predominantly congenital, not attributable to acquired neurological damage or mental illness.

quantities.quote: aphantasic participants rated their visual imagery ability on the VVIQ as being significantly lower (17.94 +/- 0.223)
only 26.22% of aphantasic participants reported a complete lack of multi-sensory imagery altogether
reported almost no ability to generate visual sensory details ... r = 0.81
aphantasia group scoring comparatively to control group 1 on the PCL-5 overall ... p = 0.776
Weak visual imagery ability is typically defined by a total score of 32 or less on the VVIQ

contributions.typing_rationale: First large-sample demonstration that aphantasia frequently extends beyond vision to other sensory modalities, reframing it as a broadly multi-sensory imagery deficit rather than a purely visual one.
Empirical finding that aphantasics dream less frequently and with reduced sensory/affective content.
Integrates the aphantasia memory deficit with a constructive-episodic-memory / future-simulation account, using imagery as the shared substrate.
Confirms, in a large cohort, prior small-sample observations that spatial imagery and navigation are spared in aphantasia.

external_baselines.description: Typical sample size of prior aphantasia studies (paper reports N=10-20).
Approximate effect sizes for group differences in prior small-sample studies (paper reports d=1.0-3.0).

deltas.note: Methodological scale advance: N=667 vs a typical prior N of ~10-20, enabling well-powered estimation of the aphantasia cognitive profile. Absolute/relative deltas are on sample size (power), not on an effect estimate.

sota.resolver_notes: Undermind semantic search (year_max=2020) on the multisensory-imagery/memory/dreaming profile returned Bainbridge 2019/21 (object-vs-spatial memory in aphantasia) as the closest finding-level prior, plus Keogh & Pearson 2017/18 (objective absence of imagery) and Zeman 2015 (naming aphantasia) as framework priors. No contemporaneous uncited near-neighbor covered the full multisensory+memory+dreaming profile at N=667; moderate neighborhood.
